newsitem.title: USA: UPS talks recess with no word of settlement.
newsitem.headline: UPS talks recess with no word of settlement.

text.p: United Parcel Service Chairman James Kelly said on Monday the company and the Teamsters were closer to a settlement of their two-week-old strike as they headed into another round of talks.
But he predicted the strike could continue for "much, much longer" if negotiations broke off this week.
"We are indeed closer than we were four days ago, but there are still some very difficult issues for them (negotiators) to discuss today," Kelly told CNN.
He was asked if he thought the strike could continue for some time if there was a breakoff in negotiations.
"Yes," he said, "if we don't conclude negotiations through these discussions this week, it certainly could go on for much, much longer."
The Wall Street Journal said in its Monday edition that the parcel delivery service's board was set to consider a plan to hire replacement workers this week.
But, Kelly told CNN, "The last thing we want to do is replace them, but the longer it goes the more options we have to consider."

Both parties are scheduled to resume negotiations at noon Monday (1600 GMT) in Washington with no word of a settlement of the two-week strike by 185,000 employees. The walkout has cost the largest U.S. package delivery company $600 million in revenues.

On Sunday evening during a brief break, Teamsters President Ron Carey urged his members to keep up the pressure. He spoke in a conference call to more than 200 locals, where rank-and-file members were listening with union officials.

"We still don't have agreements on any major issue," Carey said. He exhorted his members to prepare for everything from candlelight vigils to leaflet distributions at sports events this week to build support for the strike.
The recess came just hours after President Bill Clinton expressed optimism the parties were very close to settling their dispute.

"It's my gut feeling they'll settle," the president told reporters as he arrived at Martha's Vineyard in Massachusetts on Sunday for a three-week vacation. "They're that close," he said, holding up two fingers not very far apart.
"It's a good deal," the president added. "It will set a precedent for unions."
But the Teamsters threw cold water on the idea that the parties were anywhere near settling.
"Reports that a settlement is near are not accurate," the Teamsters said in a recorded message on voice mail. "No agreement has been reached on any major issue."

Teamsters spokeswoman Gaye Williams, in a separate interview on Monday with CNN, said. "There has not been agreement on any of the major issues" and did not give any indication the parties were close to ending the strike.
When asked what the president meant by his remarks, Williams said: "I can't speak for the president. I'm not sure what information he has."
She also announced that on Thursday the Teamsters union is having a "day of action" and urged people who support the union's position in the strike to wear blue ribbons.

Soon after the talks recessed without an agreement late Sunday, Labor Secretary Alexis Herman canceled television appearances and scuttled plans to fly to California to address the Federation of Government Employees.
UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable to have their goods delivered.
UPS officials responded to a request by the Federal Reserve Board, sending officials a detailed analysis of the strike's impact on the company and the economy.
The strikers were getting help from other unions, but were receiving only $55 a week in strike benefits.
The strike is the largest since a three-day 1976 strike by 400,000 Teamster truck drivers, according to Cornell University labor studies professor Richard Hurd.
